Canonical structure of weighted markers ​

This chapter sets out the canonical structure of weighted particle-in-cell markers and characterises every redistribution of the markers that preserves it. Its central statement is the factorisation lemma: a redistribution is symplectic if and only if it is a canonical map of positions and momenta followed by a free choice of the new weights. The next chapter asks what such maps can achieve, and the four constructions of the manual are four ways to choose the canonical map and the weights.

Weighted markers ​

Consider markers,  , of one species with mass   and charge . Marker has a position in the spatial domain ( or the torus ), a velocity   and a weight  . The markers represent the density      , with the total weight and the total momentum .

In the package a set of markers is a Markers object: vectors x, v, w for  , or   matrices x, v and a vector w. momentum, canonical, from_canonical, total_weight, total_momentum and kinetic_energy give the quantities of this chapter.

julia
using ParticleRemapping
mk = Markers([0.3, 1.2, 2.0], [0.5, -1.0, 2.0], [0.2, 0.5, 0.3]; m = 2.0)
(p = momentum(mk), P = total_momentum(mk), kinetic = kinetic_energy(mk))
(p = [0.2, -1.0, 1.2], P = 0.3999999999999999, kinetic = 1.75)

Grid moments in one dimension ​

The constructions in one spatial and one velocity dimension (1D-1V) measure the markers on a grid. The positions lie in the periodic interval , and the grid has nodes   ,  , with linear B-spline shape functions . On the cell the only non-zero shape functions are

with the index   taken modulo . They form a partition of unity,  . The grid moments of the marker set are

The grid charge is  , the grid current is  , and is the kinetic energy that the shape function collects. Because of the partition of unity,  . The grid is a PeriodicGrid, and the moments are grid_moment:

julia
using Random
Random.seed!(1)
grid = PeriodicGrid(2π, 8)
mk = Markers(2π .* rand(200), randn(200), 0.5 .+ rand(200); m = 1.0)
# the partition of unity: the moments sum to the marker sums
sum(grid_moment(grid, mk, 2)) ≈ sum(mk.w .* mk.v .^ 2)
true

The Lagrangian and the canonical coordinates ​

Inserting into the phase-space action of Low (1958) gives the particle Lagrangian of one species with an electrostatic potential (Bottino and Sonnendrücker, 2015; Kraus et al., 2017),

Its Poincaré–Cartan one-form    identifies the canonical coordinates

and the canonical symplectic form

The weight enters the canonical momentum, as it enters the Poisson structure of geometric particle-in-cell methods (Kraus et al., 2017). The Hamiltonian is

where is the potential and field energy; it depends on the weights through the charge density. In a 1D-1V particle-in-cell method with the grid potential  , depends on the markers only through the grid charge , with  . Hamilton's equations are

with   . Dividing the second equation by gives  : in the motion does not depend on the weights. For fixed weights the flow preserves .

Definition (ensemble phase space)

The single-marker phase space is (  or ) with points  . The ensemble phase space is   with points  ,  , and the form . The weights are parameters of the ensemble, not coordinates of . In matrix form, Hamilton's equations read   with   (canonical_J).

The group acts on by the translation    of every position. Its momentum map is the total momentum

which is the physical momentum of the represented density. By Noether's theorem, the flow of a Hamiltonian that is invariant under the translation conserves . Requirement (R2) of the background asks a redistribution to keep it.

The presymplectic form on weighted markers ​

A redistribution may change positions, velocities and weights. Its state space is the  -dimensional space of the states ,  . Let

be the kinematic projection onto . With Leibniz's rule,     , so the canonical form, written on the states, is the pull-back

It is closed, because it is a pull-back of a closed form, and it is degenerate. A redistribution    with   is symplectic when  .

The matrix of for 1D-1V states is presymplectic_matrix. It agrees with   (kinematic_pullback), exactly with automatic differentiation and to round-off with fourth-order central differences of step (the map is quadratic, so the truncation error vanishes):

julia
using LinearAlgebra
y0 = [0.4, -0.8, 0.25, 1.9, 1.3, 0.40]          # (x₁, v₁, w₁, x₂, v₂, w₂)
Ω = presymplectic_matrix(y0; m = 1.7)
Ω_fd = kinematic_pullback(y0; m = 1.7, jacobian = (F, y) -> fd_jacobian(F, y; order = 4))
(automatic = norm(kinematic_pullback(y0; m = 1.7) - Ω), differences = norm(Ω_fd - Ω),
 rank = rank(Ω))
(automatic = 0.0, differences = 3.9372074229455376e-11, rank = 4)

The lemma is the condition on the full state space. Two further forms are useful: one for a redistribution that is applied at fixed input weights, and one for a redistribution generated by a flow in a pseudo-time .

The gauge step ​

Every symplectic redistribution therefore splits into two steps: a canonical map of the ensemble in , and a gauge step

which moves along the kernel of . The gauge step is the identity on :    as functions on the states, whatever depends on. Hence    and   for every positive , also when depends on the state of the whole ensemble. It preserves the total momentum . The gauge step is also the only part that is not volume-preserving in : the Jacobian of   at fixed is , so a marker's -volume scales by while its weight scales by . This is the freedom that the weights add.

Read in the canonical coordinates, the gauge step is a change of weight at fixed : any new weights with the velocities

which changes the kinetic energy from to . All the symplectic content of a redistribution is therefore in the motion of ; the weights act as labels of the markers, as the charge-to-mass ratio does for several species, and the physical Hamiltonian depends on these labels. A change of weight at fixed velocity is different: it maps to , and if depends on the state its Jacobian is not symplectic in general.

The common layer implements the gauge step as gauge_step. Its pull-back residual (pullback_residual, central differences with step ) vanishes to the truncation error also for a stretch that depends on the state of the marker:

julia
λ(z) = 1 + z[1]^2 + sin(z[2]) * z[3]^2 + 0.3z[3]
gauge(z) = [z[1], λ(z) * z[2], z[3] / λ(z)]
pullback_residual(gauge, [0.3, -1.2, 0.8]; m = 1.7)
2.167743762271357e-9

Kicks, drifts and cotangent lifts ​

The following elementary canonical maps of the ensemble are exactly symplectic even when their data depend on the ensemble, because each is the time-one flow of a Hamiltonian on : a kick    with  ; a drift    with  ; and their compositions. A cotangent lift  ,   of a diffeomorphism of the spatial domain is canonical for a fixed ; in one dimension,

The cotangent lift of the gradient of a convex potential in the momenta, with the roles of and exchanged, is canonical in the same way; the sliced redistribution uses both. A kick, then a drift, followed by an arbitrary new weight, preserves , as the lemma states; so does a cotangent lift with the weight   and  :

julia
m = 1.7
function kick_drift_reweight(z)
    x, v, w = z
    P = m * w * v - sin(x)                 # kick with χ = cos x
    X = x + P^3 / 5                        # drift with η = p⁴/20
    W = 0.5 + x^2 + w * cos(v)^2           # any positive weight
    [X, P / (m * W), W]
end
φ(x) = x + 0.3sin(x)
lift(z) = [φ(z[1]), z[2], z[3] / (1 + 0.3cos(z[1]))]
(pullback_residual(kick_drift_reweight, [1.1, 0.4, 2.5]; m),
    pullback_residual(lift, [1.1, 0.4, 2.5]; m))
(9.728884364790247e-10, 4.646860674029085e-11)
